chunks: "An oscilloscope is an instrument that plots voltage against time.
The horizontal axis is time, the vertical axis is volts, and it redraws that picture continuously so I can actually watch a signal evolve instead of reading one number off a multimeter.
What makes it useful is that it shows shape. I can see a clean 3.
3 volts logic edge versus one that rings and overshoots, a power rail that has 50 millivolts of ripple on it, a glitch that lasts 20 nanoseconds, or two signals and the delay between them.
With a multimeter all of those just look like 'about 3. 3 volts.'

The specs I care about are bandwidth, which says how fast a signal the front end can pass without rounding it off; sample rate and memory depth, which say how much detail and how long a window I can capture; vertical resolution, usually 8 bits, which sets how small a change I can see; and the number of channels.
Most modern scopes are digital storage scopes: they sample the input with an ADC, store it in memory, and draw it.
The thing I always keep in mind is that the probe is part of the measurement. It adds capacitance and a ground path, so I pick the probe and the bandwidth to suit the signal."
